outline_section.section_title: Introduction to RC Circuits as Systems
outline_section.learning_goal: Set up a series RC circuit as a continuous-time system by naming the source voltage as the input and a circuit voltage as the output.

image_policy.image_description_seed: A clean textbook-style series RC circuit driven by a source voltage, with the source marked as the input and the capacitor voltage shown as the first output choice.
visual_elements: output label on the capacitor voltage $v_C(t)$
image_policy.image_generation_notes: Use a simple monochrome circuit schematic with clear labels and no decorative elements. The image should reduce the load of identifying the source, the passive components, and the output node.

tutorial_outline.direct_instruction_goal: Show that the RC circuit becomes a system once the source voltage is named as $v_s(t)$ and a circuit variable such as $v_C(t)$ is named as the output.
tutorial_outline.base_case: A series RC circuit driven by one source voltage, with the capacitor voltage used as the first output choice.
paragraph_plan: Introduce the RC circuit as an input-output model, not just a physical schematic.
Identify the source voltage $v_s(t)$ as the input signal and the chosen circuit variable as the output signal.
Connect the source, resistor, and capacitor with the circuit relation that governs the output.
Summarize the system view as a mapping from $v_s(t)$ to the chosen output and preview that later examples will change only the chosen output or the way the relation is read.

outline_section.handoff_notes: Keep the explanation at the level of model setup and circuit roles. Do not turn this section into a differential-equation exercise yet.

example_outline.worked_example_prompt: In the RC circuit, identify which signal should be treated as the input and explain why the source voltage, not $v_R(t)$ or $v_C(t)$, plays that role.

solution_step_plan: Point to the independent source and name its voltage $v_s(t)$.

Record the start of the system model as $v_s(t)$ feeding the circuit.

prompt_blocks.text: For the source-driven RC circuit shown, which signal should be treated as the input to the system?

question.correct_answer: $x(t)$ is the input because it is the driven source voltage.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: The source drives the rest of the circuit, so the input signal is the source voltage $x(t)$. Both $v_R(t)$ and $v_C(t)$ are internal responses, while $i(t)$ is the branch current, not the input signal.

prompt_blocks.text: In the RC circuit shown, with source voltage as input and capacitor voltage as output, which equation is the correct system rule?

answer_explanation_blocks.text: Use KVL first: $v_s(t)=v_R(t)+v_C(t)$. Substitute $v_R(t)=R i(t)$ and $i(t)=C\frac{d}{dt}v_C(t)$. This gives the system rule $v_s(t)=RC\frac{d}{dt}v_C(t)+v_C(t)$, mapping input $v_s(t)$ to output $v_C(t)$.

prompt_blocks.text: If the same circuit is modeled with output variable $y(t)$ instead of $v_C(t)$, and input remains $v_s(t)$, which is the correct system rule?

answer_explanation_blocks.text: This is the same physical rule with notation relabeled. The derivative term multiplies $RC$, so $v_s(t)$ equals $RC$ times the output derivative plus the output itself. Any swap of input/output or missing $RC$ factor breaks the rule.
